lead: At an ordinary point x₀, the coefficient functions of a second-order linear ODE are smooth enough for a power series. Write y = Σ aₙ(x−x₀)ⁿ, substitute, and the ODE turns into a recurrence for the coefficients aₙ. Two initial numbers, y(x₀) and y′(x₀), fix every coefficient. This method solves equations with variable coefficients that have no elementary closed form, such as y″ − xy = 0. It is the first step before Legendre and Bessel functions.
prereq: You need: 3.1 ordinary points and regular singular points, Unit 2 second-order linear ODEs, and Taylor series.

blocks.text: Write the second-order linear ODE as P(x)y″ + Q(x)y′ + R(x)y = 0. A point x₀ is ordinary when P(x₀) ≠ 0. Divide by P: y″ + p(x)y′ + q(x)y = 0, where p and q have Taylor series about x₀. Then a solution can be written as a power series about x₀. The symbol aₙ is the coefficient of (x−x₀)ⁿ; a₀ = y(x₀) and a₁ = y′(x₀). Some syllabi call this the Taylor series method. The convergence guarantee is geometric: the series converges at least up to the nearest singular point of p or q in the complex plane. For y″ − xy = 0 every point is ordinary and the radius is infinite. The method builds one coefficient at a time. It works because p and q are analytic at x₀.

blocks.where: a<sub>n</sub> is the coefficient of (x − x<sub>0</sub>)<sup>n</sup>; x<sub>0</sub> is the ordinary point; a<sub>0</sub> = y(x<sub>0</sub>) and a<sub>1</sub> = y′(x<sub>0</sub>).

items: Assume y = Σ a<sub>n</sub>(x−x<sub>0</sub>)<sup>n</sup> and differentiate term by term: y′ = Σ<sub>n=1</sub><sup>∞</sup> n a<sub>n</sub>(x−x<sub>0</sub>)<sup>n−1</sup>, y″ = Σ<sub>n=2</sub><sup>∞</sup> n(n−1)a<sub>n</sub>(x−x<sub>0</sub>)<sup>n−2</sup>.
Put these series into the ODE. Multiply out terms such as (x−x<sub>0</sub>)Σ a<sub>n</sub>(x−x<sub>0</sub>)<sup>n</sup>.
Shift indices until every series uses the same power (x−x<sub>0</sub>)<sup>m</sup>. Do not compare x<sup>m</sup> with x<sup>m−1</sup>.
Set the coefficient of each (x−x<sub>0</sub>)<sup>m</sup> to zero. The constant term gives one equation; the general m gives the recurrence.
Solve the recurrence from a<sub>0</sub> and a<sub>1</sub> upward. Initial values fix a<sub>0</sub> and a<sub>1</sub>; all later coefficients follow.

blocks.text: After substitution, two series may carry powers xᵐ and xᵐ⁻¹. Shift the index in one of them until every term carries the same power (x−x₀)ᵐ. Only then compare coefficients. The coefficient of each power must be zero because a power series that is zero on an interval has all coefficients zero. The lowest power usually fixes a₂; the general power gives a recurrence that starts from a₀ and a₁. In y″ + y = 0 the recurrence is aₘ₊₂ = −aₘ/((m+2)(m+1)), so coefficients two steps apart are coupled. In y″ − xy = 0 the extra x shifts the index once more, so the coupling is three steps apart. This is why the shift must be done before solving.

blocks.where: for y″ + y = 0; m = 0, 1, 2, …; a<sub>0</sub> and a<sub>1</sub> are free constants.

sections.h3: Reading the series and its radius

blocks.text: A second-order equation needs two independent solutions. The series with a₀=1, a₁=0 is one; the series with a₀=0, a₁=1 is the other. For y″ − xy=0 these begin y₁=1+x³/6+x⁶/180+⋯ and y₂=x+x⁴/12+⋯. Only a₀ and a₁ are free. a₂ is not free: the lowest power in y″ is x⁰ and it fixes a₂. A recurrence gives coefficients one by one; write the first four or five values and check the pattern covers all n. The two free constants match the two initial conditions. The radius guarantee uses the complex plane. A coefficient can look smooth on the real line but have a singular point at x₀±i. Example: y″ + y/(1+x²)=0 has singular points at ±i, so a series about 0 converges for |x|<1. This matters near the edge of the interval.

figure.caption: The highlighted box is the recurrence. Notice that the index shift comes before it; without the shift the coefficients cannot be compared.

spec.title: Power series at an ordinary point

examples.question: Solve y″ − xy = 0 about x = 0 with y(0) = 1 and y′(0) = 0, up to the term x⁶.
steps: Check x₀ = 0. The coefficient of y″ is 1, so P(0) = 1 ≠ 0 and x = 0 is an ordinary point. Assume y = Σ<sub>n=0</sub><sup>∞</sup> a<sub>n</sub>x<sup>n</sup>.
Apply the initial conditions: a<sub>0</sub> = y(0) = 1 and a<sub>1</sub> = y′(0) = 0.
Differentiate the series: y″ = Σ<sub>n=2</sub><sup>∞</sup> n(n−1)a<sub>n</sub>x<sup>n−2</sup>.
Substitute into y″ − xy = 0: Σ<sub>n=2</sub><sup>∞</sup> n(n−1)a<sub>n</sub>x<sup>n−2</sup> − xΣ<sub>n=0</sub><sup>∞</sup> a<sub>n</sub>x<sup>n</sup> = 0.
Shift the first series by m = n−2. Shift the second by m = n+1. The equation becomes 2a<sub>2</sub> + Σ<sub>m=1</sub><sup>∞</sup> [(m+2)(m+1)a<sub>m+2</sub> − a<sub>m−1</sub>]x<sup>m</sup> = 0.
Equate coefficients. The constant term gives 2a<sub>2</sub> = 0, so a<sub>2</sub> = 0. For m ≥ 1, (m+2)(m+1)a<sub>m+2</sub> = a<sub>m−1</sub>, or a<sub>n</sub> = a<sub>n−3</sub>/(n(n−1)) for n ≥ 3.

Compute the coefficients using a<sub>0</sub> = 1 and a<sub>1</sub> = 0: a<sub>3</sub> = a<sub>0</sub>/(3·2) = 1/6; a<sub>4</sub> = a<sub>1</sub>/(4·3) = 0; a<sub>5</sub> = a<sub>2</sub>/(5·4) = 0; a<sub>6</sub> = a<sub>3</sub>/(6·5) = (1/6)/30 = 1/180.
Assemble the series up to x⁶: y = 1 + x³/6 + x⁶/180 + ⋯. The terms x¹, x², x⁴ and x⁵ have zero coefficients.
examples.answer: The solution is y = 1 + x³/6 + x⁶/180 + ⋯ up to the term x⁶.
examples.check:
from fractions import Fraction

a = [Fraction(0) for _ in range(7)]
a[0] = Fraction(1)
a[1] = Fraction(0)
a[2] = Fraction(0)
for n in range(3, 7):
    a[n] = a[n-3] / Fraction(n * (n - 1))
for n in range(2, 7):
    print(float(a[n]))

traps: Do not compare a term with x<sup>m</sup> to a term with x<sup>m−1</sup>; shift every series to the same power first.
a<sub>2</sub> is not free. The lowest power in y″ fixes it; only a<sub>0</sub> and a<sub>1</sub> come from y(x<sub>0</sub>) and y′(x<sub>0</sub>).
The radius guarantee uses the complex plane. A real-looking coefficient can have singular points at ±i.
When differentiating y = Σ a<sub>n</sub>x<sup>n</sup>, the first series in y″ starts at n=2, not n=0; starting wrongly changes a<sub>2</sub>.

quiz.q: For a series solution about x₀=0, what are a₀ and a₁ in terms of y?
Why does setting the coefficient of each power to zero give valid equations for the aₙ?
quiz.a: A power series equal to zero on an interval has all coefficients zero; powers are linearly independent.

quiz.q: For y″ + y = 0 about x=0, write the recurrence and the first four nonzero terms with a₀=1, a₁=0.
In y″ − xy = 0, explain why a₂=0 but a₃ depends on a₀.
quiz.a: The coefficient of x⁰ is 2a₂, so a₂=0. The coefficient of x¹ is 6a₃−a₀, so a₃=a₀/6; the term xy starts at x¹, not x⁰.

quiz.q: For y″ − xy=0 with y(0)=2, y′(0)=0, find a₃ and a₆.
State the radius-of-convergence guarantee for a series about an ordinary point x₀.
quiz.a: It converges at least up to the distance from x₀ to the nearest singular point of the coefficient functions in the complex plane.

quiz.q: A student substitutes y=Σaₙxⁿ into y″ + xy′ + y = 0 and gets (n+2)(n+1)aₙ₊₂ + n aₙ + aₙ = 0. Simplify the recurrence.

beyond: Not for the exam. The same substitution gives the Airy functions Ai(x) and Bi(x) for y″ − xy=0; they appear in quantum barriers and optics. Numerical libraries compute them by solving the recurrence and summing with care. Series solutions also feed perturbation methods in orbital mechanics and control. Search next: Airy function, recurrence for power series solution, radius of convergence of series solution.
